title: Workflows and agents: who owns the control flow?

items.stem: In which of these systems does the model, rather than the programmer's code, own the control flow (the choice of what happens next)?

options.text: Code asks the model to summarize a manual page, then always sends that summary to the student.
Code asks the model to label a question, then runs the fixed handler for that label.
Code gives the model three tools, and the model picks each next call until it is done.
Code runs a fixed list of steps, and the model writes the text that each step sends.

items.stem: Every booking request at the makerspace needs the same four steps in the same order: read the request details, check the calendar for that slot, book it if it is free, and send a confirmation. The wording of requests varies a lot, but the steps never change, and the model budget is small. Which design fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow: code runs the four steps in order and calls the model only to read the request.
An agent with all four steps as tools, so the model can adapt the order for each request.
An agent, because the wording of requests differs and only a model can handle varied wording.
Four separate agents, one per step, so that every step gets its own model to make decisions.

items.stem: Which one of these makerspace tasks gives the strongest reason to use an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: A student gives a machine, a date and a time, and the assistant books that slot.
After each booking, the assistant sends a confirmation message in a set template.
Each night, the assistant lists tomorrow's bookings for the staff in one fixed format.
A student asks why a 3D print keeps failing, and which manual pages to check is unknown in advance.

items.stem: A teammate says: "Our assistant calls a language model at every step, so it is an agent." In a few words, what decides whether a system is a fixed workflow rather than an agent: who or what chooses the order of the steps in a fixed workflow?

The team is comparing designs for booking requests. The fixed workflow makes exactly 2 model calls per request. The agent design averages 5 model calls per request, because it loops. Assume every call costs the same and there are 400 requests in a week. How many more model calls does the agent design make in that week?

A design has three handlers (booking, manual question, other), each a fixed sequence of steps written in code. For each incoming message, the model's only output is one of the three labels, and the code then runs that handler. Is this a workflow or an agent, and why?

options.text: An agent, because the model's label decides what happens to each message.
A workflow, because the code fixes every path and the model only picks one of them.
An agent, because the model has to read the student's message before anything else.
Neither, because sorting messages into handlers always needs several model calls.
